cmo-cmo-2014-01.title: Telescope, then AM–GM
cmo-cmo-2014-01.body:
Let $b_0 = 1$ and $b_m = (1 + a_1)(1 + a_2)\cdots(1 + a_m)$ for $m \ge 1$. Then $b_m = b_{m-1}(1 + a_m)$, so
$$\frac{a_m}{b_m} = \frac{(1 + a_m) - 1}{b_m} = \frac{1}{b_{m-1}} - \frac{1}{b_m}.$$
Summing over $m = 1, \ldots, n$, the sum telescopes:
$$\sum_{m=1}^n \frac{a_m}{b_m} = \frac{1}{b_0} - \frac{1}{b_n} = 1 - \frac{1}{b_n}.$$
By AM–GM, $1 + a_i \ge 2\sqrt{a_i}$, so
$$b_n = \prod_{i=1}^n (1 + a_i) \ge 2^n\sqrt{a_1a_2\cdots a_n} = 2^n.$$
Therefore the sum is $1 - \frac1{b_n} \ge 1 - \frac{1}{2^n} = \frac{2^n - 1}{2^n}$, with equality when all $a_i = 1$ (then the sum is $\frac12 + \frac14 + \cdots + \frac1{2^n}$). ∎

cmo-cmo-2014-02.title: Counting squares, and a construction
cmo-cmo-2014-02.body:
Here a board has $m$ rows (of length $n$) and $n$ columns (of length $m$). Since $m, n$ are odd, every row and every column is either red-dominated or blue-dominated (no ties), and "red-dominated" for a row means at least $\frac{n+1}{2}$ red squares.

**The total $m + n$ is impossible.** The board has $mn$ squares, an odd number, so one colour is in the majority. If red is, then not every column can be blue-dominated (otherwise blue would be in the majority); if blue is, then not every row can be red-dominated. So the total is at most $m + n - 1$.

**Case $m = 1$ or $n = 1$.** Say $m = 1$ (one row, $n$ columns). Then $m + n - 1 = n$, and colouring everything blue gives $0$ red-dominated rows and $n$ blue-dominated columns. So the maximum is $n = \max(m, n)$. The case $n = 1$ is symmetric, with answer $m$. (If $m = n = 1$ the answer is $1$.)

**Case $m, n \ge 3$: the total $m + n - 1$ is impossible.** Write $m = 2a - 1$, $n = 2b - 1$ with $a, b \ge 2$. Transposing the board and swapping the colours turns red-dominated rows into blue-dominated columns and vice versa, so it suffices to rule out: *all $m$ rows red-dominated and $n - 1$ columns blue-dominated*. Each red-dominated row has at least $b$ red squares, so there are at least $mb = (2a - 1)b$ red squares. Each blue-dominated column has at least $a$ blue squares, so there are at least $(n - 1)a = (2b - 2)a$ blue squares. Hence
$$mn \ge (2a - 1)b + (2b - 2)a = 4ab - 2a - b.$$
But $mn = (2a - 1)(2b - 1) = 4ab - 2a - 2b + 1 < 4ab - 2a - b$ because $b > 1$. Contradiction. So the total is at most $m + n - 2$.

**Construction for $m + n - 2$.** Colour the first column entirely red, and the rest of the first row blue. The remaining $(m - 1)\times(n - 1)$ board has even side lengths; colour it like a chessboard, so each of its rows and columns has equally many red and blue squares. Then:
- rows $2, \ldots, m$ have one extra red square (in column $1$): red-dominated, $m - 1$ rows;
- columns $2, \ldots, n$ have one extra blue square (in row $1$): blue-dominated, $n - 1$ columns.
(Row $1$ has $n - 1 \ge 2$ blue squares and $1$ red, and column $1$ is red, so they do not count.) The total is $m + n - 2$.

**Answer:** $m + n - 2$ when $m, n \ge 3$, and $\max(m, n)$ when one of $m, n$ equals $1$.

cmo-cmo-2014-03.title: Shift all entries by a constant
cmo-cmo-2014-03.body:
Work modulo $p$ and identify $\{0, 1, \ldots, p-1\}$ with the residues mod $p$. Let $S$ be the set of tuples satisfying (i) and (ii).

**$|S| = (p - 1)p^{p-1}$.** Choose $a_1, \ldots, a_{p-1}$ freely ($p^{p-1}$ ways); then exactly $p - 1$ of the $p$ values of $a_p$ make the sum nonzero mod $p$.

**Classes.** For a tuple $a = (a_1, \ldots, a_p)$ and $k \in \mathbb{Z}_p$, let $a + k = (a_1 + k, \ldots, a_p + k)$ (entries reduced mod $p$). The sum changes by $pk \equiv 0$, so $S$ is mapped to itself, and $S$ splits into classes $\{a, a + 1, \ldots, a + (p-1)\}$ of exactly $p$ distinct tuples each (the first entries $a_1 + k$ are all different).

**Exactly one good tuple per class.** Let $u = \sum a_i \not\equiv 0$ and $v = \sum a_ia_{i+1}$ (indices mod $p$). Then
$$\sum_{i=1}^p (a_i + k)(a_{i+1} + k) = v + k\sum_i (a_i + a_{i+1}) + pk^2 \equiv v + 2ku \pmod p.$$
Since $p$ is odd and $p \nmid u$, $2u$ is invertible mod $p$, so exactly one $k \in \mathbb{Z}_p$ makes $v + 2ku \equiv 0$. Thus each class contains exactly one good tuple.

Hence the number of good tuples is
$$\frac{|S|}{p} = (p - 1)p^{p-2} = p^{p-1} - p^{p-2}.$$
(Check: $p = 3$ gives $6$, $p = 5$ gives $500$, matching a computer count.)

**Answer: $p^{p-1} - p^{p-2}$.**

cmo-cmo-2014-04.title: Radical axes and directed angles
cmo-cmo-2014-04.body:
We use directed angles between lines, $\measuredangle(\ell, m)$, taken modulo $180^\circ$; recall that four points $W, X, Y, Z$ (no three collinear) are concyclic iff $\measuredangle(YW, YX) = \measuredangle(ZW, ZX)$, with the usual convention that when two of the points coincide the chord is replaced by the tangent.

**The common angle.** Let the quadrilateral be labelled counterclockwise. For $P$ inside the convex quadrilateral, at each vertex the ray to $P$ lies inside the angle of the quadrilateral, and turning from $AP$ to $AB$, from $BP$ to $BC$, from $CP$ to $CD$, from $DP$ to $DA$ is a rotation in the same sense (clockwise) by the same amount. Hence there is one value $\theta$ with
$$\measuredangle(AP, AB) = \measuredangle(BP, BC) = \measuredangle(CP, CD) = \measuredangle(DP, DA) = \theta.$$

**The line $PR$.** Let $\omega_1 = (PAB)$ and $\omega_2 = (PCD)$. The point $R$ lies on line $AB$ and on line $CD$, so its powers with respect to $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ are $\overline{RA}\cdot\overline{RB}$ and $\overline{RC}\cdot\overline{RD}$; these are equal, both being the power of $R$ with respect to the circumcircle of $ABCD$. So $R$ lies on the radical axis of $\omega_1, \omega_2$, which is the line through their common points $P$ and $M$ (if the circles are tangent at $P$, $M = P$ and the radical axis is the common tangent). Now
$$\measuredangle(MP, MB) = \measuredangle(AP, AB) = \theta \ \ (\text{on } \omega_1), \qquad \measuredangle(MP, MD) = \measuredangle(CP, CD) = \theta \ \ (\text{on } \omega_2).$$
So the lines $MB$ and $MD$ make the same directed angle with $MP$: they coincide, and $M$ lies on $BD$. (If $M$ happens to coincide with $B$ or $D$, it lies on $BD$ trivially, and the equality $\measuredangle(MP, MB) = \theta$ or $\measuredangle(MP, MD) = \theta$ that remains meaningful is all that is used below.) Therefore line $PR$ (= line $PM$) satisfies
$$\measuredangle(PR, BD) = \measuredangle(MP, MB) = \theta .$$

**The line $PQ$.** In the same way let $\omega_3 = (PBC)$ and $\omega_4 = (PDA)$. The point $Q$ lies on lines $BC$ and $AD$, so $\overline{QB}\cdot\overline{QC} = \overline{QA}\cdot\overline{QD}$ and $Q$ is on the radical axis $PN$ of $\omega_3, \omega_4$, where $N$ is their second common point. Then
$$\measuredangle(NP, NC) = \measuredangle(BP, BC) = \theta, \qquad \measuredangle(NP, NA) = \measuredangle(DP, DA) = \theta,$$
so $N$ lies on $AC$, and $\measuredangle(PQ, AC) = \measuredangle(NP, NC) = \theta$.

**Conclusion.**
$$\measuredangle(PR, PQ) = \measuredangle(PR, BD) + \measuredangle(BD, AC) + \measuredangle(AC, PQ) = \theta + \measuredangle(BD, AC) - \theta = \measuredangle(BD, AC).$$
So the angle between lines $PR$ and $PQ$ equals the angle between the diagonals $BD$ and $AC$. ∎

cmo-cmo-2014-05.title: A strategy driven by the first number
cmo-cmo-2014-05.body:
Work with residues mod $k$; the goal is a state with **at most $k - 2$ nonzero residues**. We prove by induction on $n \ge 0$ that you can force this (for $n \le k - 2$ there is nothing to do).

**Strategy for a list $x_1, \ldots, x_n$.**
1. If at most $k - 2$ residues are nonzero, stop.
2. If $x_1 \equiv 0$, use the induction hypothesis for the list $x_2, \ldots, x_n$ (choosing only blocks inside it, which never changes $x_1$). It ends with at most $k - 2$ nonzero residues among $x_2, \ldots, x_n$, and $x_1 \equiv 0$: done.
3. Otherwise $x_1 \equiv j$ with $1 \le j \le k - 1$, and at least $k - 1 \ge j$ residues are nonzero. Choose the block from $x_1$ to the **$j$-th last nonzero number** (counting nonzero entries from the right). Call its position $p_j$; note that exactly $j - 1$ nonzero numbers lie to the right of $p_j$, and they are not changed.

$x_1$ is in every chosen block, so it changes by $\pm 1$ each step. It suffices to show that this play cannot go on forever with steps 1 and 2 never triggered. Suppose it does: then $x_1 \in \{1, \ldots, k - 1\}$ forever and there are always at least $k-1$ nonzero numbers.

**Claim.** Let $1 \le j \le k - 2$. If from some time $T$ on $x_1$ never equals $j - 1$, then $x_1 = j$ only finitely often after $T$.

*Proof.* After $T$, $x_1$ moves by $\pm 1$ and never hits $j-1$; so whenever $x_1 = j$ the answer must be "add $1$", and once $x_1 = j$ has occurred, $x_1 \ge j$ at all later times. We only look at the steps from that moment on. Consider the position $p_j$ of the $j$-th last nonzero number and the values at positions $\ge p_j$.
- At a step with $x_1 = i > j$, the block ends at the $i$-th last nonzero number, strictly left of $p_j$; nothing at positions $\ge p_j$ changes, so $p_j$ and these values stay the same.
- At a step with $x_1 = j$, the block ends exactly at $p_j$ and the answer is "add $1$": the value at $p_j$ increases by $1$ (mod $k$), positions $> p_j$ are unchanged. Either it is still nonzero ($p_j$ unchanged) or it becomes $0$, and then the new $j$-th last nonzero number is strictly to the left: $p_j$ decreases.

Since the value at $p_j$ becomes $0$ after at most $k - 1$ consecutive increments at a fixed $p_j$, each $k - 1$ visits to $x_1 = j$ decrease $p_j$. And $p_j \ge 2$ always: if $p_j = 1$, then $x_1$ itself would be the $j$-th last nonzero number, so only $j \le k - 2$ numbers would be nonzero and we would have stopped. Hence there are only finitely many visits. $\square$

**Finishing.** $x_1$ never equals $0$, so by the claim with $j = 1$, $x_1 = 1$ only finitely often; after that $x_1$ never equals $1$, so by the claim with $j = 2$, $x_1 = 2$ only finitely often; and so on up to $j = k - 2$. Hence from some time on $x_1 = k - 1$ at every step. But from $x_1 = k - 1$ the next value is $k - 2$ or $k \equiv 0$ (for $k = 2$ both are $0$) — a contradiction.

So after finitely many steps step 1 or step 2 applies, and by induction you reach a state in which at least $n - k + 2$ numbers are divisible by $k$. ∎
